q: How do widget configuration and State differ in Flutter?
a: Widgets describe immutable configuration; a State object can retain mutable state across compatible rebuilds.
explanation: The framework uses type and identity to decide whether state survives. Rebuilding widgets is normal; choose state ownership around user lifetimes rather than avoiding every build.
mistake: Assuming rebuilding always destroys all associated state.

q: A network request starts every time a Flutter widget builds. What is wrong?
a: Build can run repeatedly. Own the request in a suitable lifecycle or state layer rather than starting side effects on every build.
explanation: Cache or manage the operation for the desired lifetime and define refresh behavior. Render loading, error, and result state separately. Test parent rebuilds and navigation.
mistake: Treating build as a one-time initialization callback.
rubric: Keep rendering free of repeated side effects

q: An async result calls setState after a Flutter screen closes. How do you handle it?
a: Cancel owned work or ignore obsolete results, and check that UI state is still valid before applying it.
explanation: Dispose controllers and subscriptions. A mounted check can avoid an invalid update but does not automatically stop wasted work or prevent stale results after parameters change.
mistake: Using mounted as the entire cancellation strategy.

q: Build a long Flutter feed without rendering every item up front.
a: Use a lazy list builder with stable item identity and lightweight row builds.
explanation: Bound image decoding and caching, paginate data, and preserve appropriate scroll state. Measure frame timing; lazy widgets alone do not fix expensive work inside every visible row.
mistake: Loading all remote data because the widgets are lazy.

q: A Flutter app drops frames while parsing a large payload. Would async fix it?
a: Async does not move CPU work to another isolate. Measure parsing cost and offload suitable computation when transfer overhead is justified.
explanation: Keep UI work on its owning isolate and send transferable data. Small jobs can cost more to offload than to run locally. Validate on representative devices and payload sizes.
mistake: Equating a Future with CPU parallelism.
followups: How do you handle stale results?

q: Design Flutter state for an offline task manager with syncing.
a: Separate presentation state from repositories and durable local data, with explicit sync and conflict policies.
explanation: A state library does not determine durability. Use stable task IDs, durable pending operations, and clear error/retry states. Test app termination while saving and syncing.
mistake: Keeping the only copy of pending edits in a UI notifier.

q: A Flutter app targets mobile and desktop. What should vary by platform?
a: Share domain behavior where useful while adapting input, navigation, layout, accessibility, and platform services.
explanation: Validate plugin support, lifecycle behavior, and performance on every target. Use platform boundaries for capabilities rather than scattering platform checks throughout business logic.

q: Set a performance policy for a large Flutter product.
a: Define device-based frame, startup, memory, and network budgets, then measure representative user journeys continuously.
explanation: Keep profiling comparable across releases and make regressions actionable for owners. Approve exceptions with evidence. Optimize measured hot paths while preserving maintainability and accessibility.
mistake: Judging performance only on a flagship development device.
